title: ZooKeeper: a small tree that a whole cluster agrees on
dek: ZooKeeper stores a little data, configuration, membership, who leads, in a tree of nodes that a small ensemble of servers keeps consistent. Clients can watch nodes and have nodes vanish when they die. From those few pieces come leader election, locks and service discovery.

items: Data lives in znodes, a tree like a file system, each holding a little data (1 MB at most, usually far less). An ensemble of 3 or 5 servers keeps it consistent with its own atomic broadcast protocol (Zab).
Ephemeral znodes disappear when the client's session ends; sequential znodes get an increasing number; watches tell a client when a znode changes.
Writes go through the leader and need a majority. Reads come from the server a client is connected to and can be slightly behind.
Persistent znodes stay until deleted: `/config/payouts/batch_size`.
Ephemeral znodes belong to a client session and vanish when it ends, which is how 'this worker is alive' is represented.
Sequential znodes get a counter appended (`n_0000000017`), which gives every candidate a place in line.
Watches are one-time notifications that a znode or its children changed; the client reads again and sets a new watch (newer versions also offer persistent watches).

body.label: ZOTATO · A FEW ZNODES
body.x:
/zotato
  /config/payouts/batch_size          "500"        persistent
  /election/payouts/n_0000000017      "worker-a"   ephemeral, sequential
  /services/dispatch/10.0.4.7:8080    ""           ephemeral: present while that server's session lives
body.say: Three kinds of znode under /zotato. A persistent setting, the payout batch size, 500. An ephemeral sequential znode for worker A in the payouts election. And an ephemeral znode for one dispatch server, which disappears when its session ends, so the list of children is the list of live servers.

body.cap: Watching only your predecessor means a leader's death wakes one waiting worker, not all of them. With a thousand candidates, that matters.

items: Locks work the same way: the lowest sequential znode under `/locks/payout-42` holds the lock.
Pass the znode's number, or the session's, to whatever the leader writes to as a fencing token, so a paused old leader is refused.
Session timeouts are a trade-off: a short timeout replaces a dead leader quickly but can also expire a leader that was only slow.
Use the Curator library's recipes rather than writing these yourself.

body.cap: A write is safe once a majority has it, so five servers survive two failures. Reads are local and fast, which is why they can lag.

items: All updates from all clients are applied in one order, and each client's own operations happen in the order it sent them.
A client always sees its own writes and never goes back in time, even if it reconnects to another server.
For a read that must reflect every committed write, call `sync` first.
Everything is held in memory and every write goes through one leader, so ZooKeeper suits thousands of small writes a second, not your application's data.
Older Kafka clusters used it for metadata and controller election; Kafka 4.0 removed that dependency.
HBase, Hadoop's high-availability setup and Solr use it for masters and cluster state.
Many companies use it for service discovery and configuration.
etcd (Raft-based, used by Kubernetes) and Consul fill the same role in newer stacks.

items: Another small cluster that must be up: if the ensemble loses its majority, everything waiting on it stalls.
Careful client code for session expiry, reconnection and watches that fire once.
Limited write throughput; misuse as a database or a queue overloads it.

items: Use a coordination service for leader election, locks, membership and small shared configuration; say ZooKeeper or etcd.
Explain ephemeral sequential znodes for election, and fencing for safety.
Size the ensemble: 3 survives 1 failure, 5 survives 2.
Keep application data out of it.
Where it appears here: the Job scheduler problem uses a lease with fencing for exactly this job.

body.label: Go deeper: why one write order is enough

body.x: ZooKeeper doesn't make every read linearizable; it guarantees that all writes happen in one order and that each client sees a consistent, ever-advancing view. That turns out to be enough to build locks and elections, because the decision ('my znode is the lowest') is made from a single ordered history. Keeping reads local is what lets ZooKeeper serve many more reads than writes.
